2.47.q: Your right is to the work itself, never to its results.
2.47.m: Put your full effort into what you do, but don't make the outcome your reason for acting. Results depend on many things beyond you. Also, don't use this as an excuse to do nothing.
2.47.x: Chapter 2. Arjuna has just frozen on the battlefield. After explaining the nature of the self, Krishna turns to practical advice on how to act. This is the most quoted verse of the Gita and the seed of karma yoga.
2.47.d:
Picture the great battle about to begin at Kurukshetra. Two armies of cousins face each other. Arjuna, the finest archer, asks his friend and charioteer Krishna to drive between the armies. He sees his teachers, uncles and cousins on the other side, and his hands go weak. He drops his bow and says he will not fight.

Krishna first explains what a person truly is. Then he gives the practical advice in this verse: you cannot control how things turn out, only how you act. So do your duty fully, without being driven by fear of losing or hunger for winning, and do not run away from action either.

2.48.q: Stay steady, let go of clinging, and treat success and failure alike. That evenness is yoga.
2.48.m: Do the work from a calm centre. Win or lose, the mind stays level. Krishna defines yoga here as this balance, not as a posture.
2.48.x: Chapter 2, directly after verse 47. Krishna addresses Arjuna as Dhananjaya, one of his many names, and gives the working definition of yoga for the rest of the chapter.
2.48.d: Arjuna is still shaken, so Krishna gives him a simple way to act without being torn apart. Do the work, drop the clinging, and stay the same whether you win or lose. Krishna calls this balance yoga. For Arjuna it meant he could face the hardest task of his life with a steady mind.

2.20.q: The self is never born and never dies. When the body is struck down, it is not.
2.20.m: What you truly are is not the body. The body changes and ends, but the inner self is unborn and lasting.
2.20.x: Chapter 2. Arjuna is overwhelmed at the thought of fighting his own teachers and relatives. Krishna's first answer is not about duty but about what a person really is.
2.20.d:
Arjuna argues that no victory is worth killing his own family. He sits down in the chariot and says he will not fight. Krishna seems to smile and gently tells him the wise do not grieve for the living or the dead.

Then he shares the first big idea: the real you was never born and can never be killed. The fear of death, he says, comes from looking at the body instead of the self.

2.22.q: As we shed worn-out clothes for new ones, the embodied self leaves worn-out bodies for new ones.
2.22.m: Death is compared to changing clothes. The wearer continues, and only the garment is replaced.
2.22.x: Chapter 2, two verses after the one above. Krishna keeps consoling Arjuna with a simple everyday image.
2.22.d:
Right after that first teaching, Krishna gives Arjuna a picture he can hold in his mind. When clothes wear out, you simply change into new ones. The self does the same with bodies.

It was meant to soften grief. The people Arjuna loves are like people changing clothes, not people vanishing forever.

4.7.q: Whenever righteousness fades and wrongdoing rises, I bring myself forth.
4.7.m: When the moral order declines badly enough, the divine steps into the world to restore balance.
4.7.x: Chapter 4. Krishna explains why he has come back again and again across ages. The word Bharata addresses Arjuna as a descendant of the Bharata line.
4.7.d:
Krishna tells Arjuna this knowledge is very old. He once taught it to the sun god, it was passed down, and over time it was lost. Now he is telling it again because Arjuna is his friend and devotee.

Arjuna is puzzled: you were born recently, so how could you have taught the sun god? Krishna answers that he has had many births, and Arjuna has too, but he remembers them. Then comes this verse: whenever goodness fades and wrongdoing rises, he comes forth.

4.8.q: To protect the good, to end wrongdoing, and to set dharma firm, I appear in every age.
4.8.m: This completes the previous verse. The purpose of the divine appearance is protection, correction and restoring order.
4.8.x: Chapter 4, the verse right after 4.7. The two are usually read together.
4.8.d:
This is the second half of Krishna's answer to Arjuna's puzzle. After saying he appears when righteousness declines, he gives three reasons: to protect good people, to remove those who cause harm, and to set right living on firm ground again.

Tradition reads this as a hint about the war itself. Things had gone badly wrong, and someone had to set them right.

6.5.q: Lift yourself by yourself. Do not let yourself sink. You are your own friend, and your own enemy.
6.5.m: Your mind can be your greatest ally or your worst opponent. Be the one who lifts you up.
6.5.x: Chapter 6, on meditation. Krishna is describing how a person trains the mind, and says the effort has to come from within.
6.5.d:
In Chapter 6 Krishna teaches meditation. He tells Arjuna that nobody can do the inner work for you. You must lift yourself with your own mind.

Arjuna answers honestly: the mind is restless and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees it is hard, but says steady practice and letting go can tame it. So this verse is the encouragement before the honest struggle.

18.66.q: Let go of all other paths and come to me alone. I will free you. Do not grieve.
18.66.m: After all the teachings, Krishna offers a simple invitation: surrender with trust and let go of worry.
18.66.x: Chapter 18, near the very end. Krishna has finished explaining everything and tells Arjuna to reflect and then choose freely. This verse is his closing reassurance.
18.66.d:
The long conversation is nearly over, but Arjuna is still unsure. Krishna sums up everything and says: think it over fully, then choose as you wish. Then he gives his deepest instruction: let go of your worry about all the rules and paths, come to me, and do not grieve.

A few verses later Arjuna says his confusion is gone and he will act on Krishna's word.

18.78.q: Where there is Krishna, the master of yoga, and Arjuna with his bow, there are fortune, victory, prosperity and sound judgment.
18.78.m: The closing line: wisdom joined with committed action is where good things last.
18.78.x: Chapter 18, the final verse. It is spoken by Sanjaya, the narrator who has been describing the battlefield conversation to the blind king Dhritarashtra.
18.78.d:
Sanjaya has been telling the blind king Dhritarashtra everything happening on the battlefield, using special sight the sage Vyasa gave him. After describing Krishna's teaching and even the vision of the universal form, he ends with his own belief: where Krishna and Arjuna are together, victory and good fortune will follow.

It is also a quiet warning to the king, whose sons stand on the other side.
